meta.description: Cicero, defending Gnaeus Plancius in 54 BC. The virtue he means is gratitude — and the famous one-line “Gratitude is…” version is a later rewrite.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, orator and philosopher
answer.sourceLine: Cicero said it in court. The sentence comes from his defence speech Pro Plancio, delivered in 54 BC, at chapter 33, section 80, and this exact English wording is C. D. Yonge’s literal translation. The virtue under discussion is gratitude: the preceding sentence reads “while I wish to be adorned with every virtue, yet there is nothing which I can esteem more highly than the being and appearing grateful.” The Latin, confirmed in the text on Latin Wikisource ↗, is haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum — literally “the mother of all the remaining virtues.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 54 BC, defending Gnaeus Plancius on a charge arising from his election as aedile
haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum
C. D. Yonge (1812–1891), The Orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero, vol. 3 (London: George Bell and Sons)

source.excerpt: In truth, O judges, while I wish to be adorned with every virtue, yet there is nothing which I can esteem more highly than the being and appearing grateful. For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues. What is filial affection, but a grateful inclination towards one’s parents?
trail: The English was read first-hand in the full text of Yonge’s volume 3 ↗, which contains the sentence verbatim: “For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues.” It sits under the chapter heading XXXIII, immediately after Cicero’s remark about “the being and appearing grateful.”

The Latin was checked independently against Pro Cn. Plancio on Latin Wikisource ↗, where the section marker 80 stands immediately before “haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum” — confirming both the wording and the locator.
Latin Wikisource dates the speech to 54 BC; Wikipedia’s Cicero article ↗ places its delivery between July and September of that year.
The popular one-line version was checked too, and it is not a translation of this sentence by anyone: see the fact-check below.
source.excerptNote: Read directly from the Internet Archive scan of Yonge’s volume 3 ↗. The quoted line is the second sentence here; the first is what tells you which virtue he means.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: About Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.metaLine: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, lawyer, orator and philosopher
author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (3 January 106 BC – 7 December 43 BC) was Rome’s most celebrated advocate and, in the Republic’s final decades, one of its most exposed politicians. Pro Plancio belongs to his years after exile, and the defence is personal: Gnaeus Plancius had sheltered him in Macedonia when he fled Rome. The passage on gratitude is therefore not an abstract moral flourish — it is Cicero explaining to a jury why he is standing there at all.

misattribution.heading: The version you have probably seen
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right. The wording usually is not.

items.who: “Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all the others”
items.why: This is the form carried by the big quotation aggregators, and it is not Yonge’s sentence or any wording found in the volume read here. It silently moves the noun gratitude into the sentence from the clause before it, and drops “this one virtue.” The meaning survives the edit; the quotation does not.
The sentence is securely his, in the Latin ↗ and in Yonge’s English ↗. Only the tidied-up one-liner is someone else’s work.

misattribution.truthLine: Cicero really did call this virtue the parent of all the others, and he really did mean gratitude — but he said it in a sentence, in a courtroom, and the slogan version was assembled later.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cicero was defending the man who had sheltered him. When he fled Rome into exile in 58 BC, Gnaeus Plancius — then quaestor in Macedonia — took him in. Six years later Plancius stood accused over his election as aedile, and Cicero returned the favour in the only currency he had.

That is why the speech stops to argue that gratitude is the parent of every other virtue. It is not a detour. It is the defence: Cicero is telling the jury that a man who repays a debt is demonstrating the quality from which filial duty, patriotism, piety and friendship all descend — and that he is doing exactly that by standing up to speak.
detailsBody: The sentence that follows the quoted line shows how Cicero builds the claim. “What is filial affection, but a grateful inclination towards one’s parents?” — then good citizenship, then piety, then friendship, each recast as gratitude wearing different clothes. It is a lawyer’s argument rather than a philosopher’s: he is not proving gratitude is foundational so much as making it impossible for the jury to admire any virtue without admiring this one first.
context.pull: There is nothing which I can esteem more highly than the being and appearing grateful.

sourcesVerified.claim: Yonge's translation, vol. 3, contains verbatim under chapter XXXIII: 'For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues', immediately preceded by 'there is nothing which I can esteem more highly than the being and appearing grateful'.

The Internet Archive item orationsofmarcus03cice is 'The orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero, literally translated by C.D. Yonge', containing the orations for his House, Plancius, Sextius, Coelius, Milo and Ligarius, published in London by George Bell and Sons.

The Latin text of Pro Cn. Plancio on Latin Wikisource carries, at section marker 80 under chapter XXXIII, 'haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum', and dates the speech to 54 BC.
Wikipedia gives Cicero's dates as 3 January 106 BC to 7 December 43 BC and places the Pro Plancio defence between July and September 54 BC.
Charles Duke Yonge, the translator, lived 1812-1891.
